It is, therefore, very difficult to determine the position of stress in every word. The following rules, tentatively deduced, may be helpful to the student. ... Stress is heard in— (1) The negative prefix ad as in 'aj-jumai ... (12) Generally the first syllable as in 'tuleb-on, ‘wood, forest’ ... Stress is not heard in— ... (2) The suffix -ən or -an added to form nouns or verbal nouns ... new_statements.quote: Similarly, the comparison of word stress in Assam Sora and Orissa Sora in this chapter also reveals that both the Sora varieties have an iambic word stress in disyllables. In order to come to this conclusion three phonetic properties of word stress, namely, vowel length, pitch variation and vowel amplitude are examined in this chapter. Consequently, the acoustic correlates of these three phonetic properties, namely, vowel duration, fundamental frequency and vowel intensity provide evidence that second syllable is more prominent than the first syllable. (pp. 223-224) [Abstract, p. v:] the acoustic analysis in this work confirms that Assam Sora has an iambic stress pattern where, the second syllable is more prominent then the first syllable in disyllables.

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog record for Sora has an empty rule and there are no existing statements; this supplies a placement (second syllable of disyllables, iambic) for both the Assam and the Orissa varieties, with acoustic evidence. Not a contradiction of anything recorded.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Iambic word stress: in disyllabic words (the minimal word template; monosyllables are rare) the second syllable is the prominent one, cued by longer vowel duration, higher f0 and greater intensity. Shown acoustically for Assam Sora (Singrijhan, Sessa, Koilamari, Lamabari) and for Orissa Sora (Raiguda village, southern Orissa). p. 206 notes that before this work 'Regarding Orissa Sora, the word stress pattern is undescribed.'
new_statements.secondary_stress: not discussed; analysis limited to disyllables, nothing on longer words
new_statements.exceptions: p. 224: 'although there are a few exceptions in some cases where the results do not match the regular pattern, the patterns are largely similar across a majority of the compared data'
new_statements.identity_note: Nayak 1995 describes the Saora of the plains of Gunupur Sub-Division, Koraput (undivided) district, Orissa (p. 26). Horo 2017 covers Assam Sora (a 19th-century transplanted variety; speakers from Singrijhan, Sessa, Koilamari, Lamabari) and Orissa Sora from Raiguda village, southern Orissa; Horo & Sarmah 2015 covers Assam Sora (Singrijhan) only.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Assam Sora (Singrijhan speakers) words are minimally disyllabic; acoustic measures (second-syllable vowels longer, higher f0, greater intensity, more peripheral quality) indicate iambic stress, i.e. prominence on the second syllable of disyllables. Reports that schwa is never stressed in central Indian (Orissa) Sora.

audit.quote_check: confirmed in the copy we hold
audit.reasoning: (1) Both deciding quotations are verbatim in copies we hold at the stated places (Ramamurti 1931 djvu the text layer = Part I sec. 8 pp. 6-7 + fn. 1; Horo et al. 2023 FASAL 12 the text layerp. 144 and 445-455 p. 166). (2) The classification 'conflict' rests on the only full early description (1931 manual, impressionistic, morphology-keyed rules with default initial stress) against the only dedicated prosodic work on the language (Horo et al. instrumental series 2015-2023: exceptionless second-syllable prominence in disyllables, cues split in 3-4 syllable words, Gidugu's morphological conditioning 'being subjected to rigorous testing'). Glottolog lists no phonology of Sora proper (Merlo 1920 is Sora, Italy) and no later grammar with a fuller stress treatment; Rao 1998 sec. 2.8 (held, Srikakulam) simply restates initial/morpheme-initial accent in Ramamurti's mould. (3) downloaded now: Horo 2017
